Series::sinc¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::sinc() const
Series& Series::sinc_()
Series& Series::sinc_() const

What It Does¶

Computes the normalized sinc function elementwise:

sinc(x) = sin(pi x) / (pi x)   for x != 0,   sinc(0) = 1

The pi inside is what “normalized” means: the zero crossings land on the non-zero integers, and the function integrates to 1 over the whole line. sinc is the impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter and the continuous interpolation kernel behind Whittaker-Shannon reconstruction, so sinc() is the building block for resampling and band-limited interpolation.

Behaviour:

  • sinc(0) = 1. The 0/0 at the origin is a removable singularity and the limit value is filled in.

  • sinc(n) = 0 for every non-zero integer n (in floating point, a value within rounding of 0).

  • sinc is even: sinc(-x) = sinc(x).

  • It decays like 1/(pi x), oscillating, with the first and largest side lobe near x = 1.43, reaching about -0.217.

  • It is smooth and finite everywhere; no poles.

sinc() is out-of-place; sinc_() overwrites the current storage.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A Series with the same shape as self, each element replaced by sinc(x). sinc_() returns a reference to the mutated series.

An integral input is promoted to float64; every non-zero integer maps to a value within rounding of 0.

Gradient¶

sinc() is differentiable everywhere, including at the origin. Away from 0:

d/dx sinc(x) = ( pi x cos(pi x) - sin(pi x) ) / ( pi x^2 )

At x = 0 the derivative is 0 — sinc has a smooth maximum there — and the backward pass returns exactly 0 for that element rather than dividing by zero.

In-Place Form¶

sinc_() is the in-place sibling of sinc(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — sinc_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0});

auto& ref = x.sinc_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 3.8981718e-17]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. sinc(0) = 1; the integers are zeros; sinc(0.5) = 2/pi.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0}).sinc()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000e+00, 6.3662e-01, 3.8982e-17, -2.1221e-01, -3.8982e-17]

sinc(1) and sinc(2) are ~4e-17, floating-point zero. sinc(1.5) = -1/(1.5 pi) = -0.2122.

Example 2. sinc is even.

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5}).sinc());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.2122, 0.6366, 0.6366, -0.2122]

Example 3. The backward pass. The slope is exactly 0 at the origin and follows (pi x cos(pi x) - sin(pi x)) / (pi x^2) elsewhere.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.sinc().sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, -1.2732, -1.0000, 0.1415]

At x = 1, cos(pi) = -1 and sin(pi) = 0, so the slope is -pi/pi = -1.

Example 4. sinc_() overwrites the current storage in place.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.5, 1.0});
a.sinc_();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000e+00, 6.3662e-01, 3.8982e-17]

Example 5. The operation is elementwise, so a grid keeps its two-dimensional layout. This is useful when a table holds sampling offsets for several output locations: each cell becomes one interpolation weight without flattening the table.

auto offsets = pluss::make_series({{0.0, 0.25}, {0.5, 1.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, offsets.sinc()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 1.0000e+00 9.0032e-01 ⎤
⎣ 6.3662e-01 3.8982e-17 ⎦

Example 6. Out-of-place evaluation can start from integer sample offsets. The result promotes to float64, preserving the small floating-point residuals at the mathematical zeros instead of truncating them.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({-1, 0, 1}).sinc()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3.8982e-17, 1.0000e+00, 3.8982e-17]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • This is the normalized sinc, sin(pi x)/(pi x). The unnormalized sin(x)/x has its zeros at multiples of pi; if you want that, scale the argument by 1/pi first.

  • sinc(n) for integer n is not exactly 0 in floating point — it is a value near 4e-17. Do not test it with == 0.0.

  • The origin is handled: both the value (1) and the gradient (0) are the limit values, not NaN.

  • Integral inputs promote to float64.

  • sinc_() requires floating storage. It cannot preserve fractional results in an integral receiver; call sinc() when promotion is needed.

Summary¶

sinc() is the normalized sinc, sin(pi x)/(pi x):

  • sinc(0) = 1, even, zeros at the non-zero integers

  • smooth and finite everywhere

  • differentiable everywhere; slope 0 at the origin, otherwise (pi x cos(pi x) - sin(pi x)) / (pi x^2)

  • sinc_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::sin: the numerator, without the normalization or the removable singularity.

  • Series::i0: another smooth entire special function.
